objectives: Compare spectacle, rigid, and soft contact-lens correction, including the vertex-distance power adjustment.
Describe refractive surgery options (LASIK, PRK, SMILE) and intraocular lenses by mechanism and candidacy.
Explain orthokeratology and evidence-based myopia-control strategies.

slides.title: Spectacle lenses and contact lenses — designs and the vertex effect
slides.body:
Correcting refractive error begins with the simplest tool: the **spectacle lens**, a story that runs from the rivet spectacles of thirteenth-century Italy to **Benjamin Franklin**'s **bifocal** (c. 1784). Modern spectacle design balances optics against weight and aesthetics. **Lens material** is chosen by **refractive index** — standard **CR-39** plastic ($n \approx 1.50$), **polycarbonate** ($n \approx 1.586$, impact resistant), and **high-index** materials ($n$ up to $1.74$) that make strong prescriptions thinner. **Aspheric** surfaces flatten the lens and reduce off-axis aberration. Multifocals progress from the segmented **bifocal** and **trifocal** to the **progressive addition lens (PAL)**, which blends distance to near power smoothly but introduces unavoidable peripheral 'swim' distortion. Anti-reflective and other coatings improve transmission and durability.

A crucial optical subtlety separates spectacles from contact lenses: **vertex distance**. A spectacle sits about **12–14 mm** in front of the cornea, whereas a contact lens sits *on* it, so the vergence reaching the eye differs. The required power must be recomputed with the **effective (back-vertex) power** formula
$$F_c = \frac{F_s}{1 - d\,F_s}$$
where $F_s$ is the spectacle power, $F_c$ the contact-lens power, and $d$ the vertex distance in **metres** (positive when moving the lens toward the eye). For a $-10.00\,\text{D}$ spectacle at $d = 0.012\,\text{m}$, $F_c = -10/(1 - 0.012 \times (-10)) = -10/1.12 \approx -8.93\,\text{D}$ — almost a full diopter weaker. The effect is negligible below about $\pm 4\,\text{D}$ but clinically essential for strong prescriptions.

**Contact lenses** divide into two families. **Rigid gas-permeable (RGP)** lenses, descended from **Kevin Tuohy**'s first corneal contact lens (1948) and the **PMMA** lenses before them, are made of oxygen-permeable polymers; they vault the cornea on a **tear lens**, so they **mask corneal astigmatism** and give crisp optics, making them ideal for irregular corneas such as **keratoconus**. **Soft contact lenses** descend from the **hydrogel** invented by **Otto Wichterle** and **Drahoslav Lím** (poly-HEMA, 1961) and the later **silicone hydrogels** that dramatically raised oxygen transmissibility, quantified by the **Dk/t** value (oxygen permeability divided by thickness). Soft lenses are more comfortable and come as daily, fortnightly, or monthly disposables, in **toric** designs for astigmatism and **multifocal** designs for presbyopia. Fitting requires matching the **base curve** and **diameter** to the cornea and ensuring adequate movement and tear exchange, because the avascular cornea depends on the lens passing enough oxygen — too little risks **hypoxia**, neovascularisation, and infection (**microbial keratitis**).

slides.title: Refractive surgery and intraocular lenses
slides.body:
Surgery can reshape the eye's optics permanently. The dominant procedures reshape the **cornea**, exploiting that it carries about two-thirds of the eye's power, so small changes in corneal curvature yield large dioptric effects.

**Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)** was the first laser corneal procedure, performed after **Stephen Trokel** showed in **1983** that the **193 nm argon-fluoride excimer laser** could ablate corneal tissue with sub-micron precision and minimal thermal damage. In PRK the surgeon removes the corneal **epithelium** and the **excimer laser** ablates the underlying **stroma** to a computed profile (flattening the centre for myopia, steepening it for hyperopia). Healing is slower and more uncomfortable because the epithelium must regrow.

**LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis)**, popularised in the 1990s and building on **José Barraquer**'s keratomileusis concept and **Ioannis Pallikaris**'s flap technique, creates a thin hinged **corneal flap** (with a microkeratome or a **femtosecond laser**), lifts it, ablates the stromal bed with the excimer laser, and replaces the flap. Recovery is fast and nearly painless, which made LASIK the most common refractive procedure. Candidacy depends on adequate **corneal thickness**, a stable prescription, and the absence of **keratoconus** — screened by **corneal topography** and **tomography** (e.g. **Pentacam**), because ablating a thin or ectatic cornea risks **post-LASIK ectasia**.

**SMILE (small-incision lenticule extraction)** is the newest mainstream technique. A **femtosecond laser** alone carves a thin **lenticule** of stroma inside the intact cornea, which the surgeon removes through a small incision — no flap and no excimer laser. SMILE preserves more of the anterior corneal nerves and biomechanics, an advantage for dry eye and corneal strength, though it currently corrects mainly myopia and astigmatism.

When the problem is the **lens** rather than the cornea — or the refractive error is very high — **intraocular lenses (IOLs)** are used. Every **cataract** operation implants an IOL after **phacoemulsification**, and the implant power is computed from biometry (axial length and corneal power) using formulas such as **SRK/T**, **Holladay**, **Hoffer Q**, and **Barrett Universal II**. IOL designs include **monofocal**, **toric** (for astigmatism), **multifocal/trifocal**, and **extended-depth-of-focus (EDOF)** optics that trade some image quality for spectacle independence. In younger patients with extreme myopia who are poor laser candidates, a **phakic IOL** (e.g. the **Implantable Collamer Lens, ICL**) can be placed *in front of* the natural lens. The first IOL was implanted by **Sir Harold Ridley** in **1949**, after he noticed that aircraft-canopy acrylic splinters were inert in pilots' eyes — one of ophthalmology's great accidental discoveries.

slides.title: Orthokeratology and myopia control
slides.body:
Two of the fastest-growing areas of optometry address not how to correct established refractive error, but how to **reshape the cornea temporarily** and how to **slow the progression of childhood myopia** — a response to the global myopia epidemic.

**Orthokeratology (ortho-k, or corneal reshaping therapy)** uses specially designed **rigid gas-permeable lenses worn overnight** to flatten the central cornea, so the wearer sees clearly during the day **without any lens or surgery**. The reverse-geometry lens redistributes the corneal **epithelium** — thinning it centrally and thickening it in a mid-peripheral annulus — producing a controlled, **reversible** flattening that corrects low-to-moderate myopia. Beyond convenience, ortho-k creates a **peripheral myopic defocus** that, as discussed below, also slows myopia progression in children.

The deeper rationale comes from the science of **emmetropisation** and myopia development. The eye grows under feedback from the retinal image; the work of **Josh Wallman**, **Frank Schaeffel**, and others on chick and primate models showed that **peripheral hyperopic defocus** — a focus behind the peripheral retina — is a powerful **growth signal** that elongates the eye and drives myopia, whereas **myopic defocus** (focus in front of the retina) **slows** elongation. Conventional single-vision spectacles, which correct only the central image, may leave the periphery hyperopically defocused and thus do little to slow progression.

This insight underpins the modern **myopia-control** toolkit, now supported by randomised trials:
- **Low-dose atropine** eye drops (commonly **0.01%–0.05%**), shown in the **ATOM** and **LAMP** studies to slow myopic progression with minimal side effects at low concentration.
- **Orthokeratology**, demonstrated to slow axial elongation (the **SMART** and **ROMIO** studies among others).
- **Dual-focus and multifocal soft contact lenses** — notably the **MiSight 1 day** lens (the first FDA-approved lens for myopia control, 2019) and centre-distance multifocals — which impose myopic defocus across the retina.
- **Myopia-control spectacle lenses** with arrays of micro-lenslets, such as **DIMS (Defocus Incorporated Multiple Segments)** and **HALT** designs.
- **Increased time outdoors** (about **2 hours/day**), repeatedly associated with reduced myopia onset, possibly via light-driven retinal dopamine.

The stakes are public-health-scale: prevalence in parts of **East Asia** exceeds **80–90%** of young adults, and **high myopia** ($\le -6.00\,\text{D}$ or axial length $> 26\,\text{mm}$) carries lifelong risk of **myopic maculopathy**, **retinal detachment**, **glaucoma**, and **cataract**. Slowing childhood progression by even a diopter or two meaningfully reduces these risks — which is why myopia control has moved from the research literature into mainstream clinical practice.

question.question: A spectacle prescription is $+8.00\,\text{D}$ at a vertex distance of $12\,\text{mm}$. Using $F_c = F_s/(1 - d F_s)$ with $d = 0.012\,\text{m}$, compute the required contact-lens power in diopters, rounded to two decimals.
Which statement correctly distinguishes the three corneal refractive procedures PRK, LASIK, and SMILE?
options: All three create a hinged corneal flap and use an excimer laser on the stromal bed.

PRK ablates the stroma after removing the epithelium (no flap); LASIK ablates the stromal bed under a hinged flap; SMILE uses a femtosecond laser to remove an intrastromal lenticule with no flap and no excimer laser.
SMILE is the oldest procedure and uses the 193 nm excimer laser, while LASIK was introduced most recently.
PRK and LASIK reshape the crystalline lens, while SMILE reshapes the cornea.
question.explanation: PRK removes the epithelium and uses the 193 nm excimer laser to ablate the stromal surface directly — no flap, slower healing. LASIK first creates a hinged corneal flap (microkeratome or femtosecond laser), then ablates the underlying stromal bed with the excimer laser, then repositions the flap — fast recovery. SMILE uses a femtosecond laser alone to cut a thin intrastromal lenticule that is extracted through a small incision, with no flap and no excimer laser. All three reshape the cornea, not the crystalline lens (so option D is wrong). PRK is the oldest and SMILE the newest (so option C is reversed), and not all three use a flap (so option A is wrong).

hints: Which one removes the epithelium? Which one makes a flap? Which one extracts a lenticule?
Only LASIK ablates a stromal bed under a flap; SMILE uses no excimer laser.
slides.workedSolution: PRK: epithelium off, excimer ablation of the stromal surface, no flap. LASIK: femtosecond/microkeratome flap, excimer ablation of the bed, flap replaced. SMILE: femtosecond-cut intrastromal lenticule extracted through a small incision, no flap, no excimer. All reshape the cornea. That is option B.

question.question: A myopia-control trial reports that a treatment slows the increase in axial length from a control mean of $0.62\,\text{mm/year}$ to a treated mean of $0.31\,\text{mm/year}$. Express the slowing as a percentage reduction in the annual elongation rate.
Why might conventional single-vision minus spectacles fail to slow childhood myopia progression, and how do dual-focus contact lenses and orthokeratology address this?
options: Single-vision lenses fully correct the periphery, so they slow progression best of all.

Single-vision lenses correct central vision but can leave peripheral hyperopic defocus, a growth signal; dual-focus contacts and ortho-k impose peripheral myopic defocus, which slows axial elongation.
Single-vision lenses paralyse accommodation, which accelerates myopia.
Dual-focus lenses work only by blocking ultraviolet light, unrelated to defocus.
question.explanation: Animal and clinical research (Wallman, Schaeffel, and others) established that peripheral hyperopic defocus — image focus behind the peripheral retina — is a stimulus for axial elongation and myopia, while peripheral myopic defocus slows growth. Standard single-vision minus lenses optimise the central image but can leave the peripheral retina hyperopically defocused, providing little anti-progression benefit. Dual-focus and multifocal soft lenses (e.g. MiSight) and orthokeratology create simultaneous myopic defocus across the retina, slowing axial elongation. Option A is the opposite of the evidence; accommodation paralysis (option C) is not the mechanism; and the benefit is from defocus, not UV blocking (option D).

hints: The relevant signal is defocus in the peripheral retina, not the centre.
Hyperopic peripheral defocus speeds growth; myopic defocus slows it.
slides.workedSolution: Eye growth is guided by peripheral retinal defocus: hyperopic defocus accelerates axial elongation, myopic defocus slows it. Single-vision minus lenses fix central vision but may leave the periphery hyperopically defocused, so they do little to slow progression. Dual-focus/multifocal contacts and ortho-k impose peripheral myopic defocus, slowing elongation — option B.

question.question: Counselling parents of a fast-progressing 9-year-old myope
question.prompt: The parents of a 9-year-old whose myopia has progressed from $-1.00\,\text{D}$ to $-2.50\,\text{D}$ in 18 months ask what can be done besides 'stronger glasses each year.' Drawing on the science of peripheral defocus and emmetropisation and the evidence base (low-dose atropine, orthokeratology, MiSight dual-focus contacts, defocus-incorporated spectacles, and time outdoors), explain why simply updating single-vision glasses does not slow progression, outline two or three evidence-based myopia-control options with their mechanisms, and explain why slowing progression now matters for the child's long-term risk of conditions such as retinal detachment and myopic maculopathy.
